newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan undecided on air protest at disputed isles.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan undecided on air protest at disputed isles.

text.p: Taiwan officials met on Wednesday to decide whether to let activists fly to a deserted East China Sea archipelago in the latest challenge to Japan's disputed claim of sovereignty.

"Officials from related agencies are meeting this afternoon to discuss the issue," an official at the Civil Aeronautics Administration said by telephone. "They should come up with a final decision after the meeting."

Leaders of the private Protect-the-Diaoyus alliance were seeking to rent helicopters to fly on Friday to the uninhabited islands claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.

Activists hoped to drop flags of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government to commemorate Taiwan's October 25 Retrocession Day -- the day in 1945 on which Japan's 50-year occupation of Taiwan was brought to an end by Tokyo's World War Two defeat.
The aeronautics administration has said the group needed approvals from both Taipei and Tokyo to fly to the Diaoyus since the airspace is jointly controlled by the rival claimants.
But Taiwan's foreign ministry, mindful of escalating tensions with Tokyo, has expressed "concern" about the planned protest, the state-funded Central News Agency reported.
The ministry was urging activists to handle the sovereignty row through "rational and peaceful means" and pledged to hold further talks with Tokyo to resolve the dispute.
Two rounds of Japan-Taiwan talks, unofficial due to their lack of diplomatic ties, have failed to defuse the situation. Japan recognises only the Beijing government, Taiwan's rival.
On October 7, Taiwan and Hong Kong activists pierced a Japanese maritime cordon and hoisted flags of the communist People's Republic of China and the Taiwan republic on the islands.
Tokyo voiced regret for what it called the illegal landing and vowed to take necessary measures to stop similar actions.

Japanese rightists have triggered an angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from ethnic Chinese across Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a lighthouse on the islands in July to assert Tokyo's claim.
Taiwan fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing waters near the islands.
The Japanese patrols also repulsed earlier attempts to land Taiwan and Hong Kong protesters on the islands, deepening anti-Japanese resentment in Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau and the communist mainland.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion with China or Taiwan.
China and Taiwan say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's defeat in World War Two.
